transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
President Trump is campaigning for Republican candidates two weeks before the midterm elections.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports Trump was in Kansas yesterday and today will go to North Carolina.
On paper, this is not really where the leader of the Republican Party should be, spending
his time and energy.
Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and yet polls suggest
it's possible.
There's a trip to a conservative corner of Iowa.
That's a state where Democrats could flip the governor's office, three of four House
seats and the Senate seat because of how unpopular Republicans are.
Trump is visiting North Carolina, as many Republican outside groups have basically gone
dark on the airwaves because the Senate race is viewed as a lost cause.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reporting.
NPR has learned that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin
Netanyahu yesterday in Israel.
Netanyahu is leading his party and seeking office again in Israeli elections, set for
later this month.
Saudi Arabia has canceled an annual investment forum.
It draws the world's most powerful hedge fund managers and bankers to the country.
It is the latest high-profile event Saudi Arabia has called off since Houthi rebels
in neighboring Yemen fired deadly attacks on the Saudi capital.
And Pierre's Ayyab Batrawi has more.
The Future Investment Initiative Forum, which oversees what's widely known as Davos in
the Desert, announced that its annual forum in Riyadh will be held next year, instead of
next week.
It gave no explicit reason for the cancellation.
It comes as Saudi airstrikes on Yemen's Houthis and missile strikes by the Iran-backed group
on Saudi airports have led to a spate of events being canceled in the kingdom.
This investment forum in particular is intertwined with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's
international clout as the man overseeing one of the world's biggest sovereign wealth
funds.
The fund runs the exclusive investment forum, with tickets running $15,000 a person.
Past attendees have included JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, BlackRock's Larry Fink, and Donald
Trump Jr.
Ayyab Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
French officials impose curfews overnight in parts of France.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports France's prime minister says local authorities can
counter who he calls delinquents and thugs.
The curfew includes Paris's Place de la République, a central gathering point that has seen some
of the worst skirmishes between protesters and police, as well as disruption and looting.
The mayor of Nice announced a curfew specifically for young people.
There are also restrictions in some northern cities, including Lille, which saw its town
hall broken into over the weekend.
President Emmanuel Macron and his government are being blamed for the mayhem.
Far right leader Marine Le Pen said the interior minister was not prepared and should resign.
The prime minister says ultra-left radical groups are trying to create chaos ahead of
the next presidential election.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A federal judge is ordering that a Saudi Arabian citizen remain jailed.
Abdul Rahman Al-Fazan is accused of planting a secret recording device in a conference
room of his employer, OpenAI.
He was detained just before he was scheduled to return to Saudi Arabia.
Federal prosecutors allege Al-Fazan often contacted a member of the Saudi royal family.
The latest U.N. climate summit has opened in Armenia.
Most delegates are working to find agreement on how to limit global warming.
The U.S. Supreme Court has announced it will again take up the issue of race and school
admissions.
This time it's focused on several middle schools in Montgomery County, Maryland, a suburb of
Washington, D.C.
And Pierre Sequoia Carrillo has more.
Three years after the Supreme Court struck down affirmative action in college admissions,
it will consider the issue of race in admissions for four selective middle schools.
The case focuses on the school's shift to a lottery system that the county says ensures
fair admissions opportunities for all students.
A group of parents who sued disagree.
They say it discriminates based on race, specifically against Asian-American students.
The case has been dismissed twice by lower courts, but will be argued sometime before
the court's term ends next summer.
Sequoia Carrillo, NPR News.
This year's World Series is set that Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians last
night to clinch the American League pennant.
Tampa will now face the Milwaukee Brewers in the fall classic.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.
Iowans, you can register to vote at any time.
Election Day is Tuesday, November 3rd, sponsored by Civic Futures Fund.

topics.text: President Trump campaigns for Republican candidates in Kansas and North Carolina before midterms
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth meets Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel
Saudi Arabia cancels its annual Future Investment Initiative investment forum in Riyadh
French officials impose overnight curfews in parts of France amid youth unrest and looting
Federal judge orders Saudi citizen Abdul Rahman Al-Fazan held over alleged OpenAI bugging
U.N. climate summit opens in Armenia as delegates seek agreement on limiting warming
Supreme Court to hear case on race in admissions at Montgomery County, Maryland middle schools
Tampa Bay Rays beat Cleveland Guardians to clinch American League pennant, face Brewers in World Series
